name: Lamentations
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text:
She weeps through the night, with tears wetting her face.
No one who loved her is left to offer comfort.
Her own friends betrayed her
and became her enemies.

Judah{c} has been dragged away in misery, in hard labor.
Now she lives among strangers and finds no home.
Her chasers caught up with her
where the road was too narrow to escape.

The roads leading to Zion{d} mourn, since nobody travels them to reach the festivals.
Her gates stand empty, and her priests sigh.
Her young women are grieving, and she tastes only bitterness.

Her opponents now give the orders, and they are relaxed and safe.
Yahweh sent this pain because her sins were so many.
Her small children walked away in front of the enemy,
taken as prisoners.

Everything lovely has drained out of Zion’s daughter.
Her officials are like starving stags that wander without any pasture.
They stumbled away with no power,
while the hunters stayed on their heels.

Jerusalem remembers, in these days of pain and wandering,
every good thing she had long ago.
Her people fell into enemy hands, and no one helped her.
Her enemies looked at her ruin and laughed.{e}

Jerusalem sinned terribly, so she has become a thing people shun.{f}
Those who once honored her now look down on her.
They have seen her shame.
She groans and turns her face away.

Her filth clings to her clothes.
She never thought about how it would end.
Her fall was shocking, and no one is there to comfort her.
She prays, “Yahweh, see how I suffer! The enemy acts so proud.”

The enemy reached out his hand
and took all her treasures.
She saw foreign nations walk into Your holy place,
people You had told never to enter Your assembly.{g}

All her people sigh while they look for something to eat.
They give up their valuables for a bite, to keep breathing.
“Yahweh, notice me and think about it: I am treated as if I were nothing.”

“Does this mean nothing to you who walk by?{h}
Look closely. Has anyone ever hurt like this?
Yahweh brought this pain on me
on the day His anger burned hot.

He sent fire from high up, and it sank into my bones.
He laid a net for my feet and forced me backward.
He left me desolate, ill from morning to night.

My sins were tied together like a heavy yoke,{i}
and His hand fastened it on my neck.
My strength gave out.
The Lord handed me over to people I cannot fight.

The Lord rejected all the mighty men inside my walls.
He summoned a crowd against me to break my young fighters.
The Lord stepped on Judah’s virgin daughter
the way workers tread grapes in a winepress.

For these things I weep.
My eyes overflow with tears.
The one who could comfort and revive me is far away.
My children are shattered, since the enemy has the upper hand.”

Zion holds out her hands, but no one comforts her.
Yahweh has ordered the neighbors of Jacob{j} to be his enemies.
Jerusalem has become something unclean among them.

“Yahweh is right,” she says, “because I would not listen to what He told me.
Hear me, peoples everywhere, and look at my pain.
My girls and my young men
have been marched away as captives.

I called to my allies, but they let me down.
My priests and elders died in the city
while they searched for food to stay alive.

Look, Yahweh, how upset I am!
My stomach is in knots, and my heart is turned upside down,
because I have rebelled so badly.
Outside, the sword kills my children.
Inside the house, death is waiting.

People heard me groan, but no one comforted me.
All my enemies heard about my trouble, and they are glad You did it.
Bring on the day You promised,
and let them end up just like me.

Let all their wickedness come before You,
and deal with them the way You dealt with me
for my many acts of rebellion.
I sigh again and again, and my heart is weak.”

notes.text: This chapter is an acrostic poem. Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. English cannot copy that pattern.
The Hebrew word is Eykah, “How!” It is the cry of someone at a funeral, and it is the Hebrew name of this book.
Judah means “praise.” Here it stands for the people of the southern kingdom.
Zion is another name for Jerusalem or its hill. The meaning is uncertain.
The Hebrew word is rare. It may mean “her ending” or “her ruin.”
Hebrew nidah. It may mean “something people shake their heads at” or “unclean.”
See Deuteronomy 23:3.
The Hebrew of this line is hard to read. It may also mean “May this not happen to you.”
A yoke is a wooden bar that fits over the necks of work animals. The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
Jacob means “he grasps the heel.” Here it means the people of Israel.

verses.text:
Without pity the Lord swallowed up every home in Jacob.
In His fury He knocked down the strong towns of Judah’s daughter.
He threw her kingdom and her rulers to the ground and shamed them.

Like an enemy, He pulled back His bow and held His right hand ready like a foe.
Everyone who was a joy to look at, He struck down.
On Zion’s daughter’s tent He emptied His fury like a fire.

The Lord acted like an enemy and swallowed up Israel.
He swallowed all her palaces and wrecked her strong towns.
He piled up mourning and crying in Judah’s daughter.

He ripped apart His own booth as if it were a garden shed and ruined the place where He met His people.
In Zion, Yahweh made festivals and Sabbaths slip from memory.
In hot anger He cast off king and priest alike.

The Lord pushed His altar away and disowned His sanctuary.
Zion’s palace walls He put into enemy hands.
The enemy shouted inside Yahweh’s house as though it were a feast day.

Yahweh planned to tear down the wall of Zion’s daughter.
He measured it out and did not stop until it was wrecked.
He made the outer wall and the inner wall cry together, and both fell apart.

Her gates have sunk into the ground.
He snapped her bars in pieces.
Her king and princes are scattered among the nations, and there is no teaching.
Her prophets cannot get a vision from Yahweh any longer.

The elders of Zion’s daughter sit silently on the ground,
with dust on their heads and rough cloth around their bodies.
The girls of Jerusalem hang their heads low.

I have cried until my eyes are tired, and my stomach is churning.
My heart spills out onto the ground over the ruin of my people,
as little ones and nursing babies pass out in the town squares.

They cry to their mothers, “Is there any grain or wine?”
They collapse like wounded soldiers in the city squares.
Their lives drain away on their mothers’ laps.

What can I say to you? What can I compare you to, Jerusalem’s daughter?
Who can I match you with, to comfort you, virgin daughter of Zion?
Your wound is as huge as the sea. Who can heal you?

Your prophets saw only false and empty visions.
They never pointed out your sin so that you could change.
Their messages were lies that led you astray.

All who pass by clap at you in scorn.
They hiss, and they shake their heads over Jerusalem’s daughter:
“Was this the city people called the most beautiful,
the delight of all lands?”

Every enemy of yours sneers at you with a wide mouth.
They hiss and grind their teeth, saying, “We have gobbled her up!
We waited for exactly this day, and now we see it.”

Yahweh carried out His plan.
He finished the word He ordered in ancient days.
He broke you down and showed no mercy.
He let your enemy celebrate and made your opponents strong.

Their hearts call out to the Lord.
O wall of Zion’s daughter, let tears pour down like a flowing stream by day and by night.
Give yourself no break, and let your eyes have no rest.

Rise up! Call out through the night as each watch begins.
Empty out your heart like water before the Lord’s face.
Reach out your palms to Him to save your little ones’ lives,
those who are fainting with hunger on every street corner.

“Look, Yahweh, and think: have You ever done this to anyone?
Must mothers eat the fruit of their own wombs, the babies they held?
Should a priest and a prophet be cut down inside the Lord’s own sanctuary?

Boys and old men lie in the dust of the lanes.
My girls and my young men fell to swords.
You put them to death when Your anger came. You slaughtered and did not spare.

You called terrors against me from every side, as if to a festival.
On the day of Yahweh’s anger no one escaped or survived.
The children I raised and cared for, my enemy has destroyed.”

notes.text: This is another acrostic poem, with verses starting in Hebrew alphabet order. Here the order of two letters is swapped, as in chapters 3 and 4.
The footstool most likely means the Ark of the Covenant, or the temple.
A horn stands for strength, like the horn of a bull.

verses.text: I am the man who has seen suffering under the rod of Yahweh’s anger.{a}
He drove me away and made me walk in darkness, not in light.
Again and again, all day long, He has turned His hand against me.
He has made my skin and flesh wear out. He has broken my bones.
He has built a wall of bitter pain and hardship around me.
He has made my home a dark place, the kind where the long-dead rest.
He has fenced me in, and I cannot walk out. He has weighed me down with heavy chains.
Even when I shout for help, my prayer is blocked from reaching Him.
He has blocked my road with cut stones and made my paths twist and turn.
He is like a bear waiting for me, like a lion hiding in the brush.
He dragged me off my path, tore me apart, and left me ruined.
He drew His bow and set me up as the target for His arrows.
He shot arrows from His quiver deep inside me.
I have become a joke to everyone. They sing mocking songs about me all day.
He has stuffed me with bitter food and made me drink bitter poison.{b}
He ground my teeth into gravel and pushed my face into the ashes.
Peace has been taken from me. I cannot remember what it feels like to be happy.
So I said, “My strength is finished. Everything I hoped for from Yahweh has gone.”
Remember how I suffer and wander, how bitter and poisonous it is.
I think about it constantly, and I feel crushed.
But one thing I remember gives me hope again:
Yahweh’s faithful love never runs out.{c} His compassion never comes to an end.
They are new every morning. How great is Your faithfulness!
“Yahweh is my share in life,” I tell myself. “So I will keep waiting for Him.”
Yahweh is good to those who wait for Him, to the one who looks to Him.
It is good to be quiet and wait while Yahweh brings rescue.
A young man does well to learn to carry a yoke.
Let him sit by himself and say nothing, because Yahweh has put this load on him.
Let him put his face in the dust. There may still be hope.
Let him offer his cheek to the one who strikes him and take all the shame.
The Lord does not reject people forever.
Even when He causes pain, He then shows compassion, because His faithful love is huge.
He does not enjoy making people suffer or causing them grief.
To crush all the prisoners of the land under foot,
to deny a person his rights before the Most High,
to cheat someone in court: the Lord does not approve of any of this.
Who can give an order and see it done, unless the Lord commanded it?
Do hard times and good times not both come from the mouth of the Most High?{d}
So why should any living person complain when he is paying for his sins?
Let us look closely at how we live and come back to Yahweh.
Let us lift up our hearts along with our hands to God in heaven.
“We have turned against You and refused to obey, and You have not pardoned us.
You covered Yourself in anger and ran after us. You cut us down and showed no pity.
You wrapped Yourself in a cloud, so no prayer could pass through.
You made us scraps and rubbish among the nations.”
All our enemies speak against us with mouths stretched wide.
Fear and traps have come on us, with ruin and destruction.
My eyes shed streams of water over the destruction of my people.
My eyes will pour out tears and will not stop,
until Yahweh looks down from heaven and sees.
What I see makes my soul ache over all the young women of my city.
Enemies who hated me for no cause chased me like a bird.
They shut me alive in a pit and threw stones over me.
The flood rose above my head, and I said to myself, “I am finished.”
From the deepest part of the pit, Yahweh, I cried out to You by name.
You listened when I spoke. You did not turn Your ears away from my plea for help.
You came near on the day I called, and You said, “Do not be afraid.”
Lord, You argued my case and rescued my life.
Yahweh, You have seen the wrong people did to me. Take up my cause.
You saw how they took revenge and made plans against me.
Yahweh, You heard their insults and every plan they made against me.
What my attackers whisper and mutter against me goes on all day.
Look at them! Sitting down or standing up, I am the subject of their songs.
Yahweh, give them back what they deserve for the things they have done.
Put a hard heart on them, and let Your curse fall on them.
Chase them in Your anger and wipe them out from under Yahweh’s sky.

notes.text: This chapter is an acrostic too. Each group of three verses starts with the same Hebrew letter, so there are 22 groups.
The Hebrew names a bitter plant, wormwood. It may also mean a poison.
Hebrew chesed, a faithful love that stays loyal to a promise.
The Hebrew has “evil” and “good.” Here it means troubles and blessings.

verses.text:
The gold has lost its shine. The best metal has turned dull.
Sacred gems lie spilled at the head of every street.{a}

The precious people of Zion were as valuable as pure gold.
Now they are counted as clay pots, the work of a potter.

Even wild jackals bare their breasts to feed their pups.
My people’s daughter has become harsh, like the ostrich in the wilderness.

The nursing baby’s tongue clings to his mouth for thirst.
Little ones beg for bread, and nobody breaks any for them.

Those who ate the best food are starving in the streets.
Those who grew up in royal purple now lie on piles of ashes.

The punishment of my people is greater than the sin of Sodom,
which was wrecked in a flash, with no hands to help.

Her princes were cleaner than snow and brighter than milk.
Their skin was ruddier than rubies, and their looks were like sapphire.

Now their faces are darker than soot, and no one recognizes them on the street.
Their skin hangs tight over their bones, dry like old wood.

Death by sword was better than death by hunger.
The hungry slowly fade away, with nothing from the fields to keep them alive.

Compassionate women cooked their own children with their own hands.
The little ones became their mothers’ meal when my people fell.

Yahweh poured out all His rage and burning anger.
He lit a fire in Zion that burned down her foundations.

The kings of the earth did not believe it, and neither did anyone in the world,
that enemies could march through the gates of Jerusalem.

It happened because of the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests,
who spilled the blood of good people inside her walls.

They wandered blind through the streets, so stained with blood
that no one dared touch their clothes.

People shouted at them, “Go away! You are unclean! Go! Do not touch us!”
So they ran off and wandered. Among the nations they heard, “You cannot stay with us.”

Yahweh Himself scattered them and no longer looks after them.
No one respects the priests or shows kindness to the elders.

Our eyes wore out looking for help that never came.
From our tower we watched for a nation that could not save us.

They hunted our steps, and we could not walk in our own streets.
Our end came near, our days ran out, and the end had come.

Those who chased us were swifter than eagles flying overhead.
They hounded us over the hills and lay in wait for us in the wilderness.

Yahweh’s anointed king, the breath of our lives, was caught in their traps.
We had said, “Under his shadow we will live among the nations.”

Be happy and celebrate, Edom’s daughter,{b} you who settle in Uz.{c}
The cup is coming around to you as well. You will drink until you are drunk, and then you will be uncovered.

Daughter of Zion, your punishment is over. He will not keep you in exile.
But Edom’s daughter, He will deal with your guilt and expose your sins.

notes.text: The stones may be the temple’s stones or the jewels of the temple treasure. The Hebrew is unclear.
Edom means “red.” The Edomites were the people descended from Esau, Israel’s neighbors to the south.
Uz may be near Edom. The meaning of the name is uncertain.

verses.text:
Yahweh, remember what has come over us.{a}
Look, and notice how we are shamed.

Strangers have taken our land,
and foreigners live in our houses.

We have lost our fathers, so we are orphans.
Our mothers have lost their husbands.

Our drinking water comes only if we pay silver for it.
Even our firewood has a price.

Pursuers are right behind us, with their hands on our necks.{b}
We are worn out and get no rest.

We made deals with Egypt and Assyria
to get enough food to eat.

Our ancestors sinned and are gone,
and now we are carrying the weight of their guilt.

Slaves are our rulers now,
and no one can free us from their hands.

We risk our lives to find food,
because of the sword in the desert.

Our skin is burning like an oven
from the fever of hunger.

Women are attacked in Zion,
and girls in the towns of Judah.

Princes are hanged by their hands,
and no one respects the elders.

Young men must grind grain at the mill,{c}
and boys fall down under loads of wood.

Elders no longer gather at the gate,
and the young have put away their music.

The joy in our hearts is gone.
Our dancing has turned into mourning.

The crown has dropped from our heads.
Woe to us, because we have sinned!

For this reason our hearts are weak,
and for this our eyes have grown dim:

Mount Zion is empty and in ruins,
and jackals{d} walk around on it.

But You, Yahweh, are King forever.
Your throne stands through every age.

Why do You forget us for good?
Why have You left us alone so long?

Yahweh, bring us back to You, and we will come back.
Make our days new again, like in the past,

unless You have turned us down completely
and are too angry with us to forgive.{e}

notes.text: This chapter has 22 verses, the same number as Hebrew letters, but it is not an acrostic.
The Hebrew is uncertain. It may be “A yoke is on our necks.”
The Septuagint says, “The chosen men lifted up their voice in weeping.”
Or “foxes.”
The Hebrew of this last verse is hard to understand. Some read it as a hopeful prayer, and others as a sad question.
